{{Short description|Probability measure on a complex plane}}
{{expert needed|mathematics|reason=review the article|date=October 2019}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Brown measure''', named after [[Lawrence G. Brown]], is a [[probability measure]] generalizing the normalized eigenvalue-counting measure (also called normalized (random) trace). It is in the same way closely related to the spectral counting measure and is a useful tool for analyzing [[Spectrum of a matrix|spectrum]] and [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenvalues]] of infinite dimensional linear operators in a von Neumann algebra.<ref name=":0">{{Cite arXiv |last1=Bruce |first1=Driver |last2=Brian |first2=Hall |last3=Kemp |first3=Todd |date=25 Aug 2020 |title=The Brown measure of the free multiplicative Brownian motion |volume=3 |pages=2–3 |class=math.PR |eprint=1903.11015 }}</ref>

== Conventions and notation ==
This article uses the following conventions and notations.

* <math>\mathcal{P}( S )</math> is the [[power set]] of the set <math>S</math>.
* <math>E( T )</math> is the [[eigenspace]] of the linear operator <math>T</math>,
* <math>| T | := \sqrt{T^{\dagger} \cdot T}</math> is the operator modulus of the [[Linear map|linear operator]] <math>T</math>.
* <math>\Delta</math> is the Laplacian in a distributional sense and <math>\Delta_{z} f( z ) := \Delta f</math> for a function <math>f \in C^{2}( \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C} )</math> where <math>\mathbb{C} \cong \mathbb{R}^{2}</math> is treated as [[Real number|real]] [[vector space]] meaning in conventional notation <math display="inline">\Delta_{z} f( z ) = \frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}f( z )}{\mathrm{d}\Re( z )^{2}} + \frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}f( z )}{\mathrm{d}\Im( z )^{2}}</math>.
* <math>\delta_{z}</math> for a <math>z \in \mathbb{C}</math> is the [[Dirac delta function]].
* <math>\det</math> is the [[Determinant|determinant function]].
* <math>\ln = \log_{e}</math> is the [[natural logarithm]].

== Motivation ==
The spectrum and eigenspace of a [[Complex number|complex]] linear operator provides a lot of information about the linear operator itself such as invertibility,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |title=Invertible Matrix Theorem |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/InvertibleMatrixTheorem.html |access-date=2026-08-08 |website=mathworld.wolfram.com |language=en}}</ref> asymptotic behavior under potentiation e.g. via the spectral radius<ref>{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |title=Spectral Radius |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/SpectralRadius.html |access-date=2026-08-08 |website=mathworld.wolfram.com |language=en}}</ref>, and much more. In larger or even infinite dimensions finding these properties can be quite a challenging task. The same is true in a weaker form for their distributions so knowing them can be useful.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |title=Eigenvalue |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Eigenvalue.html |access-date=2026-08-08 |website=mathworld.wolfram.com |language=en}}</ref>

Given a <math>n \in \mathbb{N}</math>-dimensional quadratic complex matrix <math>M \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}</math> its eigenvalues <math>\lambda_{1},\, \ldots,\, \lambda_{n}</math> are given by the zeros of its [[characteristic polynomial]] <math>\chi_{M}{:}\, \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C},\, \lambda \mapsto \det( \lambda \cdot I - M )</math> (including multiplicities)<ref name=":1" /> allowing us to formulate a probability [[measure space]] <math>( \mathbb{C},\, \mathcal{A},\, \mathbb{P} )</math> with a [[Σ-algebra|<math>\sigma</math>-algebra]] <math>\mathcal{A} \subseteq \mathcal{P}( \mathbb{C} )</math> and probability measure<math display="block">\mathbb{P}{:}\, \mathcal{A} \to [ 0,\, 1 ],\, A \mapsto \frac{1}{n}\cdot \sum_{k = 1}^{n} \delta_{\lambda_{k}}( A )</math>(the normalized eigenvalue-counting measure) assigning each set <math>A \in \mathcal{A}</math> a weighted sum of the number of <math>M</math>s eigenvalues in <math>A</math>.<ref name=":2">{{Cite arXiv |last1=Hall |first1=Brian |last2=Kemp |first2=Todd |date=26 Jul 2019 |title=Brown Measure Support and the Free Multiplicative Brownian Motion |pages=8–9 |class=math.FA |eprint=1810.00153 }}</ref> This means that if for the eigenspace, which in finite dimension is equal to the spectrum, <math>E( M )</math> and a set <math>A \in \mathcal{A}</math> is <math>\mathbb{P}( A ) = 1</math> [[if and only if]] <math>\mathbb{P}( A ) = 1</math>.

As useful as this construction is in finite dimensions, it fails in infinite dimensions for one the determinant of an infinite-dimensional linear operator might be undefined, the spectrum and eigenspace must not be equal, can each have infinite [[cardinality]] and thus can't define the normalized eigenvalue-counting measure. But to still characterize the eigenvalues and the spectrum a generalization is needed. One of these generalization called ''Brown measure''.

Another approach is needed. Define<math display="block">u{:}\, \mathbb{C} \setminus E( M ) \to \mathbb{C},\, z \mapsto \frac{1}{n} \cdot \ln( | \det( z \cdot I - M ) | ).</math> Now by using the relation <math display="inline">\det( \lambda \cdot I - M ) = \prod_{k = 1}^{n} ( z - \lambda_{k} )</math>, <math display="inline">\forall ( x_{k} )_{k \in \mathbb{N}_{\leq n}} \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{n}{:}\, \ln( \prod_{k = 1}^{n} x_{k} ) = \sum_{k = 1}^{n} \ln( x_{k} )</math> and <math display="inline">\forall ( x_{k} )_{k \in \mathbb{N}_{\leq n}} \in \mathbb{C}^{n}{:}\, | \prod_{k = 1}^{n} x_{k} | = \prod_{k = 1}^{n} | x_{k} |</math> the function <math display="inline">u</math> reduces to<math display="block">\forall z \in \mathbb{C} \setminus E( M ) \to \mathbb{C}{:}\, u( z ) = \frac{1}{n} \cdot \ln( | \det( z \cdot I - M ) | ) = \frac{1}{n} \cdot \ln\left( \prod\limits_{k = 1}^{n} | z - \lambda_{k} | \right) = \frac{1}{n} \cdot \sum\limits_{k = 1}^{n} \ln( | z - \lambda_{k} | ). </math> Now using the same probability measure space as before <math>( \mathbb{C},\, \mathcal{A},\, \mathbb{P} )</math> we can rewrite this as<math display="block">\forall z \in \mathbb{C} \setminus E( M ) \to \mathbb{C}{:}\, u( z ) = \frac{1}{n} \cdot \sum\limits_{k = 1}^{n} \ln( | z - \lambda_{k} | ) = \int_{\mathbb{C}} \frac{1}{n} \cdot \sum\limits_{k = 1}^{n} \ln( | z - w | ) \cdot \delta_{\lambda_{k}}( w )\, \mathrm{d}w = \int_{\mathbb{C}} \ln( | z - w | ) \cdot \frac{1}{n} \cdot \sum\limits_{k = 1}^{n} \delta_{\lambda_{k}}( w )\, \mathrm{d}w = \int_{\mathbb{C}} \ln( | z - w | )\, \mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}( w ). </math> Now by applying the complex Laplacian <math display="inline">\Delta</math> in the distributional sense gives <math display="block">\Delta u = \int_{\mathbb{C}} \Delta_{z} \ln( | z - w | )\, \mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}( w ) = \int_{\mathbb{C}} 2 \cdot \pi \cdot \delta_{w}\, \mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}( w ) = 2 \cdot \pi \cdot \mathbb{P}.  </math> Brown worked on [[von Neumann algebra]]s and found that given a tracial von Neumann algebra <math>A</math> with a faithful, normal, normalized tracial state <math>\tau{:}\, A \to \mathbb{C}</math> the linear operator satisfying this relation is <math>\mathbb{C} \setminus E( M ) \to \mathbb{C},\, \tau( \ln( | z \cdot I - T | ) )</math> with <math>| T | := \sqrt{T^{\dagger} \cdot T}</math> as the operator modulus. And for a matrix <math>T</math> in this von Neumann algebra became <math display="inline">\mu_{T} = \frac{1}{2 \cdot \pi} \cdot \Delta \tau( \ln( | z \cdot I - T | ) ) </math> to be known as the ''Brown measure''.<ref name=":0" />

==Definition==

Let <math>\mathcal{M}</math> be a finite von Neumann algebra equipped with a faithful, normalized normal trace <math>\tau{:}\, \mathcal{M} \to \mathbb{C}</math> so is the Brown measure of a <math>T \in \mathcal{M}</math> defined by <math display="block">\mu_{T} := \frac{1}{2 \cdot \pi} \cdot \Delta_{z} \tau( \ln( | z \cdot I - T | ) ).</math><math display="inline">u_{T}{:}\, \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C},\, z \mapsto \tau( \ln( | z \cdot I - T | ) ) </math> is [[subharmonic function]] that can also be written in terms of the [[Fuglede−Kadison determinant]] <math>\Delta_{\text{FK}}</math> as <math display="inline">u_{T}( z ) := \ln( \Delta_{\text{FK}}( T - z \cdot I ) ) </math>.

Another notation for the Brown measure is <math display="inline">B_{T} </math>.<ref name=":2" />

== Properties ==
<math display="inline">\mu_{T} </math> forms a probability measure of the <math>W^{\ast}</math>-probability space <math>( \mathcal{M},\, \tau )</math>. Formally: If <math display="inline">T \in \mathcal{M} </math> and <math>\mathcal{A} \subseteq \mathcal{P}( \mathbb{C} )</math> is a <math>\sigma</math>-algebra on <math>\mathbb{C}</math> so is <math>( \mathbb{C},\, \mathcal{A},\, \mu_{T} )</math> a probability measure space.

We have <math display="inline">\forall n \in \mathbb{N}_{0}{:}\, \int_{\mathbb{C}} z^{n}\, \mathrm{d}\mu_{T}( z ) = \tau( T^{n} ) </math> and if <math display="inline">T \in \mathcal{M} </math> is inverteble <math display="inline">\forall k \in \mathbb{Z}{:}\, \int_{\mathbb{C}} z^{k}\, \mathrm{d}\mu_{T}( z ) = \tau( T^{k} ) </math>.

For all <math display="inline">T \in \mathcal{M} </math> is <math display="inline">\mu_{T} </math>.compactly supportet. The spectrum of a <math display="inline">T \in \mathcal{M} </math> contains <math display="inline">\mu_{T} </math>s support (<math display="inline">\operatorname{supp}( \mu_{T} ) \subseteq \operatorname{spec}( T ) </math>).

For all <math display="inline">A,\, B \in \mathcal{M} </math> is <math display="inline">\mu_{A \cdot B} = \mu_{B \cdot A} </math>.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3">{{cite arXiv |last1=Campbell |first1=Andrew |title=The fractional free convolution of $R$-diagonal elements and random polynomials under repeated differentiation |date=2024-03-14 |pages=6 |eprint=2307.11935 |last2=O'Rourke |first2=Sean |last3=Renfrew |first3=David |class=math.PR }}</ref>

=== Relations to other measures ===
Let <math>n \in \mathbb{N}</math>, If <math display="inline">T \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n} </math> so is Browns measure the normalized eigenvalue-caunting measure <math display="inline">\mu_{T}{:}\, A \mapsto \frac{1}{n} \cdot \sum_{k = 1}^{n} \delta_{\lambda_{k}}( A )</math> where <math>\lambda_{1},\, \ldots,\, \lambda_{n}</math> are the eigenvalues of <math>T</math> including multiplicity according to its characteristic polynomial.<ref name=":2" />

If <math display="inline">T \in \mathcal{M} </math> is self-adjoint so is Brown measure the spectral measure.

If <math display="inline">T = c_{t} \in \mathcal{M} </math> is a circular Brownian motion so is Brown measure the uniform probability measure on the disk of radius <math display="inline">\sqrt{t} </math>.<ref name=":0" />

Given a Haar unitary element <math display="inline">U </math> the Brown measure is the normalized [[Haar measure]] <math display="inline">\text{haar} </math> on the  complex unit circle <math display="inline">\mu_{U} = \frac{1}{2 \cdot \pi} \cdot \text{haar}_{\{ z \in \mathbb{C} \mid | z | = 1 \}} </math>.<ref name=":3" />

Besides the trivial relation to the [[Lebesgue measure]] <math display="inline">\lambda_{2} </math> given by its definition the is also the relations: If <math display="inline">\mathfrak{c} </math> is a circular element and <math display="inline">T \in \mathcal{M} </math> is <math display="inline">\ast </math>-free of <math display="inline">\mathfrak{c} </math> so is

* the Brown measure <math display="inline">\mu_{T + \mathfrak{c}} </math> [[Absolute continuity|absolutely continues]] with respect to the Lebesgue measure <math display="inline">\mu_{T + \mathfrak{c}} \ll \lambda_{2} </math> on <math display="inline">\mathbb{C} </math>,
* the densityof <math display="inline">\mu_{T + \mathfrak{c}} </math> with respect to <math display="inline">\lambda_{2} </math> is strictly positive and analytic on <math display="inline">\operatorname{supp}( \mu_{T} ) </math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Campbell |first1=Andrew |last2=O’Rourke |first2=Sean |last3=Renfrew |first3=David |date=2024-07-01 |title=The fractional free convolution of R-diagonal elements and random polynomials under repeated differentiation |url=https://doi.org/10.1093/imrn/rnae062 |journal=International Mathematics Research Notices |volume=2024 |issue=13 |pages=10189–10218 |doi=10.1093/imrn/rnae062 |issn=1073-7928}}</ref>
